newsitem.title: UK: EC may seek insurance for all ships - official.
newsitem.headline: EC may seek insurance for all ships - official.

text.p: The European Commission will introduce compulsory marine insurance for all ships entering European ports if the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) does not propose adequate regulations, an EC official said on Thursday.

Stefan Lindstrom, EC official for the Directorate General VII unit for Maritime Safety and Pollution Prevention, told an insurance industry conference in London that insuring ships, their passengers and cargo was a fundamental requirement.
"We are looking for an internationally based agreement, but if it is going to take years at IMO we will go it alone," said Lindstrom.
Lindstrom said the issue of mandatory third party liability insurance had been raised by a number of maritime states and was also under discussion at IMO.
The Legal Committee of IMO would report on the issue in April and the EC would prefer an IMO initiative, but it would move ahead if IMO did not propose an international approach, he said.

He added that the EC was also aware of the UK's intention to take unilateral action over the issue in the Merchant Shipping and Maritime Security Bill which looks set to be given assent when an election is called later this year.

"The introduction of European legislation imposing mandatory third party liability insurance as a requirement for all ships wishing to call at a European port should be designed with a view to the exclusion of substandard ships from Community waters and ports," Lindstrom said.
Lindstrom added that compulsory insurance would also encourage competitiveness among European shipowners and ensure that all European citizens had the same rights across Europe.
"I see no reason why coastal states should accept that ships without adequate insurance cover should use their waters," he added.
Lindstrom said the EU was considering four main lines of action concerning compulsory marine insurance.

Port state control inspectors would check that ships entering European ports carried valid insurance certificates and would subject the vessel to detailed structural inspection if the paperwork was not presented.

The EU would consider publishing lists of companies which insure substandard ships, and was currently checking a sample of 250 vessels to see if there were any trends concerning P&I clubs which provide insurance for poor quality vessels, he told the conference.
Lindstrom said passenger ships would be treated separately to ensure that all passengers travelling between EU ports should have the same rights in an accident.
He added that the Commission was also considering whether to certify P&I clubs and similar marine insurers to ensure that compensation was available when needed.
